content: Blog Posts Less is More: Refactoring the CAR Signaling Domain 10.27.2026 What will drug discovery look like when intelligence is abundant? Our small team is an experiment that began with this question. Eight months in, we’re excited to share some first results and the story behind them. In vivo CAR T & signaling domain compression Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) reprogram the immune system to kill cancer cells. Expressed on the surface of T-cells, CARs connect an extracellular binder that targets a tumor antigen to an intracellular signaling domain that triggers the T-cell’s response. Much of CAR engineering focuses on the binder, while signaling domains largely follow a few established designs. CAR T therapy traditionally involves collecting a patient’s T-cells, engineering them outside the body, and infusing them back. In vivo CAR T simplifies this process by delivering genetic instructions directly into T-cells inside the body. Payload size matters in this setting. With mRNA delivery, a smaller payload means more molecules at the same mass dose. 1 So we asked: Can we design a smaller signaling domain that preserves function? 1 mRNA encodes instructions for T-cells to produce CARs and display them on their surface. Introducing mRNA into cells is called transfection . An alternative is to integrate DNA encoding the CAR into the cells’ genome. We use mRNA transfection throughout our experiments. Figure 1. Generations of CAR signaling domains trend toward increased length and complexity. CD3ζ delivers the primary activation signal through three immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs), short motifs whose tyrosines are phosphorylated when the CAR binds its antigen, recruiting kinases that switch on the T-cell. Costimulatory domains such as CD28 and 4-1BB add signals that sustain T-cell expansion and persistence. The second-generation architecture is still most widely used today. Our refactored signaling domain is just 45 amino acids, 70% shorter than the second-generation design. For comparison, we used a second-generation CAR whose signaling domain combines 4-1BB costimulation with CD3ζ activation. We call this architecture BBζ . In just a few months, the team developed a refactored 2 signaling domain that did more with less: one-third the length of BBζ , with improved CAR expression and T-cell function. 2 In software, refactoring changes how code is organized while preserving its function. Here, we apply the idea to CAR signaling domains. Rational design at scale Using Claude Code, we built an agent harness that orchestrates LLM reasoning and computational tools with a focus on structured outputs and observability. Scientists could steer and critique the exploration, inspect the evidence behind each design, and compare candidate sequences and their rationale. We drove the system toward a bold question: What if we rethought signaling domains from the ground up? Figure 2. Example signaling-domain designs from round 1. Click on a sequence to see a summary of the agent’s reasoning trace. Each design represented a hypothesis about how signaling function might be preserved in a smaller construct, complete with supporting evidence, reasoning, and assumptions. Through iterations of review and steering, we selected 186 designs for the initial round of testing. In many ways, this process resembled traditional rational design before the advent of ML methods, where experts, guided by hypotheses, manually inspected sequences and introduced intentional edits. The problem with that approach was scale, which we can now solve with agents. Mapping the space of signaling domains We tested the initial designs in Jurkat cells, measuring NFAT activation and tonic activation 3 . To our surprise, dozens of refactored designs produced higher on-target activation than BBζ , with lower tonic activation. 3 Jurkat cells are a human T-cell line used to screen signaling. NFAT activity is a readout of T-cell activation. Tonic activation is signaling in the absence of the target antigen. FIGURE 3. The initial screen of 186 signaling domain designs in Jurkat cells. NFAT activation is shown against tonic activation, relative to BBζ (dashed lines). Colors denote construct length. Many short designs produced high on-target activation and low tonic activation. Target: BCMA; binder: ddBCMA D-domain. We selected the top designs for testing in donor-derived primary T-cells. Across a range of effector-to-target (E:T) ratios (the number of T-cells per target cell), we measured IFN-γ secretion and killing 4 of BCMA-positive myeloma cells. Several refactored designs performed comparably to BBζ . 4 IFN-γ (interferon gamma) is a cytokine measured as a readout of T-cell activation. Killing is measured through residual luminescence: a light signal from surviving target cells, with less light indicating more killing. Figure 4. Primary T-cell validation of 10 designs against BBζ .
